Triggers.value: Visible injuries or wounds on others

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I spend long hours on my phone, games, or internet to avoid thinking
keep mind occupied all the time

Threat.value: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere
My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger

Memory.value: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish

Negative Appraisals.value: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore
My life has been destroyed by the trauma
What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it

issues.item: Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Social Contacts' is inconsistent as written: it is phrased like a trigger ('seeing people...') rather than a strategy the patient uses. Within the Maladaptive Strategies node, the other items are clear coping behaviours, so this item is internally mismatched.

issues.item: Self-Harm Distraction: I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event
issues.explanation: Self-harm used specifically as a distraction is not impossible, but in this profile it stands out as clinically poorly integrated with the rest of the selected items. The other strategies are avoidance/disengagement (screen use, avoiding people), and the threat/memory profile is hypervigilance plus overwhelm. This item introduces a much more extreme coping style without supporting indicators elsewhere in the five target components, making the strategy set feel internally uneven for the same patient.

issues.item: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: For a police-related trauma in a 46-year-old civilian graphic designer, self-blame for 'the way I acted' is possible, but here it sits awkwardly beside appraisals that frame the trauma as globally ruining life and draining meaning, without any other items suggesting perceived responsibility, moral failure, or a specific behavior during the event. The appraisal set is therefore less coherent than the other nodes.

vignette: Kaius had always taken pride in his work as a graphic designer, but after that fateful night two years ago, everything changed. He had been driving home from a late-night shift when he was pulled over by the police for a minor infraction. What ensued was a brutal and unprovoked beating at the hands of the officers, leaving Kaius with severe injuries and a deep sense of trauma. As he recalled that night, Kaius's mind would flood with unwanted thoughts – images of his own battered face staring back at him, the crunching sound of bones breaking, and the feeling of helplessness as he lay on the ground. These intrusive memories would hit him without warning, triggered by something as mundane as a visible injury or wound on someone else, be it in real life or even on TV. The sight would instantly transport him back to that fateful night, leaving him overwhelmed with emotion. In an attempt to avoid these distressing thoughts, Kaius had developed a few strategies. He spent hours scrolling through his phone, playing games, or browsing the internet – anything to distract himself from the memories and emotions that threatened to engulf him. Social interactions became increasingly difficult for him; he began avoiding people altogether, including close friends and family members. Even at work, he found it challenging to collaborate with colleagues, opting instead to focus on solo projects. Kaius's daily life was now defined by a constant sense of threat. He could never fully relax, even in the safety of his own home or office, always on high alert for potential danger. His body remained perpetually tense and ready to react, like a coiled spring waiting to be triggered. Before entering any new space, he would meticulously scan the area for possible escape routes – a habit that had become second nature. When attempting to recount the events of that fateful night, Kaius struggled to put his thoughts into words. He'd start strong but soon lose his train of thought, unable to articulate the details without becoming overwhelmed by emotion. It was as if the memories were too raw, too painful to confront head-on. The trauma had fundamentally altered Kaius's worldview. Nothing seemed meaningful anymore – not his work, not his relationships, nothing. He felt like a part of him had been irreparably destroyed, leaving behind only anger and resentment. What happened that night was deeply unjust, and the fact that no one had been held accountable gnawed at him constantly. Kaius's wife, Rachel, had tried to be supportive, but even she couldn't fully grasp the extent of his suffering. As Kaius became increasingly withdrawn, their relationship began to fray. His lack of intimacy, both physical and emotional, was starting to take its toll on their marriage. It was this realization – that he risked losing the one person who truly cared for him – that finally brought Kaius to seek help. Sitting in his therapist's office, Kaius felt a mix of trepidation and hope. He was terrified of confronting the memories and emotions he'd been avoiding for so long but also desperate to reclaim some semblance of control over his life. As he looked at the blank canvas in front of him – a stark reminder of his abandoned passion for graphic design – Kaius knew that this journey would be arduous, but he was willing to face it head-on, no matter how daunting the task seemed.
